questions.enonce_markdown:
Explain the fallacies most clearly committed in the following:

(i) The head mistress let a late-comer with mild visual impairment into class even though all the other late comers were outside on punishment.

(ii) A woman after ten years into marriage is unable to conceive and bear children. Her family members attribute her misfortune to the fact that her husband has not yet paid her dowry.

(iii) Given that each player of the team is very good, it means the team must be very good.

(3 x 3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Appeal to pity** (*argumentum ad misericordiam*), together with an inconsistent application of the rule.

The head mistress admits one late-comer because of her **visual impairment**, a circumstance that is **not relevant** to the rule about lateness (a mild impairment does not explain or excuse arriving late). The decision rests on sympathy, not on a good reason, and it treats equals unequally: the other late-comers were punished for exactly the same fault. A sound reason would show that the impairment actually caused the delay and would apply the same exception to everyone in that case.

**(ii) False cause** (*non causa pro causa*, also called questionable cause).

The family links two events, the unpaid dowry and the childlessness, **without any evidence of a causal connection**. A social arrangement such as a dowry has no physical effect on conception, while childlessness has biological and medical causes that should be investigated. Events that merely occur at the same time, or one after the other, are wrongly treated as cause and effect.

**(iii) Composition.**

The argument reasons from the **parts to the whole**: a property of each member ("very good") is attributed to the group ("the team is very good"). A team's quality also depends on organisation, coordination, tactics and the relations between players, so a group of excellent individuals can play badly together.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Construct valid standard form syllogisms from the following inferences.

(i) Given that no drunkards are doctors, it follows that no drunkards are Muslims since all doctors are Muslims.

(ii) Many boys are men since every father is a man and some boys are fathers.

(2 x 3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Method.** Identify the conclusion (the statement after "it follows that" or before "since"), then the major term (predicate of the conclusion), the minor term (subject of the conclusion) and the middle term (absent from the conclusion). Write the major premise first, then the minor premise, then the conclusion, and test the mood and the figure.

**(i) "No drunkards are doctors; all doctors are Muslims; so no drunkards are Muslims."**

- Conclusion: *No drunkards are Muslims* (E). Minor term $S$ = drunkards, major term $P$ = Muslims, middle term $M$ = doctors.

| | Statement | Form |
|:-|:-|:-:|
| Major premise (A) | All doctors are Muslims. | All $M$ are $P$ |
| Minor premise (E) | No drunkards are doctors. | No $S$ are $M$ |
| Conclusion (E) | Therefore, no drunkards are Muslims. | No $S$ are $P$ |

This is **AEE-1** (the middle term is subject of the major premise and predicate of the minor premise: figure 1). Test: the major term "Muslims" is **distributed in the conclusion** (predicate of an E proposition) but **undistributed in the major premise** (predicate of an A proposition). The syllogism commits the fallacy of **illicit major**, so it is **invalid as stated**. A counter-example of the same form with true premises: *All dogs are animals; no cats are dogs; therefore no cats are animals* (checked with Python: the form has counter-models).

**A valid syllogism built from the same premises.** The premises do support a different conclusion. The premise "No drunkards are doctors" is equivalent to "No doctors are drunkards" (simple conversion of E), and one obtains:

| | Statement | Form |
|:-|:-|:-:|
| Major premise (E) | No doctors are drunkards. | No $M$ are $P$ |
| Minor premise (A) | All doctors are Muslims. | All $M$ are $S$ |
| Conclusion (O) | Therefore, some Muslims are not drunkards. | Some $S$ are not $P$ |

with $S$ = Muslims, $P$ = drunkards, $M$ = doctors. This is **EAO-3** (*Felapton*), valid in traditional logic (it presupposes that doctors exist). The rules are respected: "drunkards" is distributed in the major premise and in the conclusion; "doctors" is distributed in both premises; one negative premise gives a negative conclusion. The original conclusion "no drunkards are Muslims" does **not** follow.

**(ii) "Many boys are men since every father is a man and some boys are fathers."**

Conclusion: *Some boys are men* ("many" is read as "some", a particular quantity), so $S$ = boys, $P$ = men, $M$ = fathers.

| | Statement | Form |
|:-|:-|:-:|
| Major premise (A) | All fathers are men. | All $M$ are $P$ |
| Minor premise (I) | Some boys are fathers. | Some $S$ are $M$ |
| Conclusion (I) | Therefore, some boys are men. | Some $S$ are $P$ |

This is **AII-1** (*Darii*). The middle term "fathers" is distributed in the major premise (subject of A); no term is distributed in the conclusion, so there is no illicit process; there is no negative premise; the particular premise gives a particular conclusion. The syllogism is **valid** (no counter-model found by Python).

questions.enonce_markdown:
Given p: *"Mary is sleeping"*; q: *"Roseline is reading"*; r: *"Janet is cooking"*, symbolise the following:

(i) Either Janet is cooking, or Mary is sleeping and Roseline is reading.

(ii) Either Mary is not sleeping and Janet is cooking, or Roseline is reading.

(iii) Roseline is reading and Janet is not cooking provided Mary is sleeping.

(3 x 2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The comma in (i) and (ii) shows which connective is the main one.

**(i)** "Either Janet is cooking, **or** (Mary is sleeping and Roseline is reading)": the main connective is the disjunction.

$$r \vee (p \cdot q)$$

**(ii)** "Either (Mary is not sleeping and Janet is cooking), **or** Roseline is reading": the main connective is again the disjunction, and the negation applies to $p$ only.

$$(\sim p \cdot r) \vee q$$

**(iii)** "Roseline is reading and Janet is not cooking **provided** Mary is sleeping": "provided" introduces the **antecedent** of a conditional, so "Mary is sleeping" is the antecedent and the whole conjunction is the consequent.

$$p \supset (q \cdot \sim r)$$

questions.enonce_markdown:
Demonstrate the following on truth tables

(i) $(\sim q \equiv \sim p) \vee (p \supset \sim r)$

(ii) $q \supset p$

(2 x 2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** Three variables, so $2^3 = 8$ rows. The main connective is the disjunction; the first disjunct is true when $p$ and $q$ have the same truth value.

| $p$ | $q$ | $r$ | $\sim q$ | $\sim p$ | $\sim q \equiv \sim p$ | $\sim r$ | $p \supset \sim r$ | $(\sim q \equiv \sim p) \vee (p \supset \sim r)$ |
|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| T | T | T | F | F | T | F | F | **T** |
| T | T | F | F | F | T | T | T | **T** |
| T | F | T | T | F | F | F | F | **F** |
| T | F | F | T | F | F | T | T | **T** |
| F | T | T | F | T | F | F | T | **T** |
| F | T | F | F | T | F | T | T | **T** |
| F | F | T | T | T | T | F | T | **T** |
| F | F | F | T | T | T | T | T | **T** |

The compound is **false only in the row $p$ = T, $q$ = F, $r$ = T** (first disjunct false because $\sim q$ is T and $\sim p$ is F; second disjunct false because $p$ is T and $\sim r$ is F). It is true in the other seven rows, so the statement form is **contingent**.

**(ii)** Two variables, so $2^2 = 4$ rows. A conditional is false only when its antecedent is true and its consequent false; here the antecedent is $q$ and the consequent is $p$.

| $p$ | $q$ | $q \supset p$ |
|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| T | T | **T** |
| T | F | **T** |
| F | T | **F** |
| F | F | **T** |

The statement form $q \supset p$ is **false only when $q$ is T and $p$ is F**; it is true in the other three rows, so it is **contingent**.
